item.title: Sri Lanka’s IRD surpasses 2026 revenue target after Customs
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: The government has revised up the 2026 total tax revenue target to Rs.5,478bn from Rs.4,910bn
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s main tax collector, the Inland Revenue Department (IRD), surpassed its 2026 revenue target of Rs. 2,402 billion this week, the government said, a month after the island nation’s Customs breached its goal for this year.

The IRD surpassed the target on Monday (16) after successfully collecting Rs. 2,441.9 billion.

The Finance Ministry quoting the IRD said the revenue collection has increased by Rs. 491 billion compared to November 16, 2025, representing a growth of 115 percent.

“The growth reflects strengthened tax administration, greater efficiency in tax revenue collection, and a growing inclination among the public to comply with tax laws and regulations,” the Finance Ministry said.

Sri Lanka Customs has already surpassed its 2026 revenue target of Rs. 2,207 billion on October 13, and it has collected Rs. 2,469 billion as of Tuesday (17).

“Revenue collected in excess of targets by government revenue-collecting agencies provides financial strength to reduce the government’s debt burden and lower debt interest payments,” the Finance Ministry said.

Sri Lanka has already revised up its 2026 tax revenue by 11.6 percent to Rs. 5,478 billion. Originally, the government had estimated Rs. 4,910 billion revenues from taxes for this year.

The island nation’s tax revenue is expected to increase 15.5 percent of the gross domestic products (GDP) this year, more than double from what it was in 2022 when Sri Lanka declared bankruptcy. (Colombo/November 19/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka MP defends stalled Rs100mn pet cemetery promised in last budget
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Promised in previous budget to house stray dogs from Colombo and its suburbs and provide cemetery and cremation services
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka parliamentarian Lakshman Nipuna Arachchi defended progress on a 100 million rupee budget-allocated dog shelter in the Piliyandala-Kesbewa area, stating that land release and legal procurement procedures caused delays but insisting the funds were not wasted.

The exchange took place in parliament after an opposition lawmaker questioned whether the government had built the facility promised in the previous budget to house stray dogs from Colombo and its suburbs and provide cemetery and cremation services.

“I am asking Lakshman Nipuna Arachchi by name whether you all at least built that pet facility,” Samagi Jana Balawegaya MP Nallin Bandara questioned, noting that 100 million had been allocated for the project in last year’s Budget.

Sri Lanka budget 2026: cemetery and cremation facilities for pets

Responding in parliament, Nipuna Arachchi acknowledged implementation hurdles but maintained that work had not halted.

Nipuna Arachchi said the selected site belonged to the Public Trustee and required formal release before the government could proceed with strict legal procurement processes.

“We got those released in the proper manner, and after that, we carried out the necessary procurement work. It hasn’t stopped,” Nipuna Arachchi claimed, adding that preliminary structural work is currently underway at the site.

“That means the money has not been completely wasted,” he said. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)

item.title: Fitch upgrades 6, affirms 2 Sri Lankan insurers’ IFS ratings on scale recalibration
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The insurers' National Ratings take into consideration their creditworthiness relative to those of other issuers in the
item.content:encoded:
Fitch Ratings – Colombo – 19 Nov 2026: Fitch Ratings has taken the following actions on the National Insurer Financial Strength (IFS) Ratings on eight Sri Lankan insurers following recalibration of the agency’s Sri Lankan national rating scale following the recent sovereign rating upgrade:

— Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation Life Limited (SLIC Life): National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘AA-(lka) from ‘A+(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— Sri Lanka Insurance Corporation General Limited (SLIC General): National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘AA-(lka) from ‘A+(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— HNB Life PLC: National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘A+(lka) from ‘A(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— HNB General Insurance Limited (HNBGI): National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘A+(lka) from ‘A(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— People’s Insurance PLC: National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘A+(lka) from ‘A(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— Co-operative Insurance Company PLC (CICPLC): National IFS Rating upgraded to ‘BB+(lka)’ from ‘BB(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— Continental Insurance Lanka Limited (CILL): National IFS Rating affirmed at ‘A(lka)’; Outlook Stable

— Construction Guarantee Fund (CGF): National IFS affirmed at ‘BB(lka)’; Outlook Stable

The insurers’ National Ratings take into consideration their creditworthiness relative to those of other issuers in the country. National scale ratings are a risk ranking of issuers in a particular market designed to help local investors differentiate risk. Sri Lanka’s national scale ratings are denoted by the unique identifier ‘(lka)’. Fitch adds this identifier to reflect the unique nature of the Sri Lankan national scale. National scales are not comparable with Fitch’s international rating scales or with other countries’ national rating scales.

The national scale recalibration reflects changes in the relative creditworthiness of Sri Lankan issuers after Fitch upgraded Sri Lanka’s Long-Term Local-Currency Issuer Default Rating (IDR) to ‘B-‌’ with Stable Outlook from ‘CCC+’ on 22 September 2026. For details, see “Fitch Ratings Recalibrates Sri Lanka’s National Rating Scale”, dated 21 October 2026.

Key Rating Drivers
The National Rating upgrades are driven by the upgrade of Sri Lanka’s Long-Term Local-Currency IDR and the recalibration of the national rating scale and greater room for positive differentiation on the recalibrated national rating scale. The National IFS Rating upgrades of SLIC Life, SLIC General, HNB Life, HNB General, People’s Insurance and CICPLC reflect their relative creditworthiness, as differentiated by their company profiles, capitalization and financial performance.

We believe the sovereign’s credit profile improvement has reduced insurers’ investment and liquidity risks, which are closely linked to those of the sovereign and domestic banks because insurers’ investment portfolios are dominated by local-currency fixed-income government securities, corporate debt and deposits with financial institutions.

SLIC Life

SLIC Life’s rating upgrade reflects its ‘Favorable’ company profile, strong capitalization and strong profitability. SLIC Life and SLIC General are fully owned by the government of Sri Lanka.

Its company profile is supported by its long operating history, extensive franchise and broad distribution network, including a strong agency force. SLIC Life has remained Sri Lanka’s third-largest life insurer for the past three years, with a stable 14% share of life-insurance gross written premiums (GWP).

Capitalization remains a rating strength. SLIC Life maintained a risk-based capital (RBC) ratio above 400% during 2023-2025 and reported a ratio of 478% at end-1H26, exceeding those of Fitch-rated domestic life-insurance peers. SLIC Life’s average return on equity (ROE) of 16% over 2024-2025 has supported internal capital generation.

SLIC General

SLIC General’s rating upgrade reflects its ‘Favorable’ company profile, strong capitalization and strong profitability.

Its company profile is supported by its long operating history, leading franchise and broad distribution network. SLIC General has retained its position as the largest non-life insurer in Sri Lanka since 2024, with a 20% share of non-life GWP in 2025.

Capitalization remains a rating strength. SLIC General maintained an RBC ratio above 250% over the past two years and reported a ratio of 265% at end-1H26 which remains stronger than that of Fitch-rated domestic non-life-insurance peers. SLIC General’s average ROE of 12% and combined ratio of 103% during 2024-2025 compared favorably with Fitch-rated domestic non-life peers, although performance was weighed down by Cyclone Ditwah-related claims in 2025. Fitch expects gradual underwriting improvement through stronger claims management, and pricing discipline.

HNB Life and HNBGI

The upgrades of HNB Life and its wholly owned subsidiary, HNBGI, reflect the group’s ‘Favorable’ company profile, strong group profitability and satisfactory capitalization. Fitch expects HNB Life to provide capital support to HNBGI, if needed, to maintain adequate capital buffers and support business growth.

Their franchises benefit from their association with the parent, Hatton National Bank PLC (National Long-Term Rating: AA-(lka)/Stable), one of Sri Lanka’s largest private commercial banks. HNB Life was the sixth-largest life insurer, with an 8.6% share of life GWP in 2025, while its average GWP growth over 2023-2025 of 30% exceeded the industry average of 19%. HNBGI was the sixth-largest non-life insurer, with a 7.3% share of non-life GWP.

HNB Life’s average ROE was 19% during 2023-2025 while the group’s average ROE of 18% reflects strong profitability. HNBGI’s operating performance has improved, with its annualized ROE rising to 10% in 1H26 from an average of 8% in 2023-2025. Its combined ratio improved to 106% in 1H26, although its three-year average of 109% remained below the industry average.

The group’s capitalization is satisfactory. HNB Life’s RBC ratio remained above 250% in 2023-2025, although below the life-insurance industry average. HNBGI’s RBC ratio declined to 198% by end-1H26, from 219% in 2024.

People’s Insurance

The upgrade reflects People’s Insurance’s improving underwriting performance and strong capitalization.

Its company profile benefits from the People’s brand and its relationship with parent People’s Leasing & Finance PLC (National Long-Term Rating: AA-(lka)/Stable), which supports distribution and contributes materially through the group channel. It is Sri Lanka’s eighth largest non-life insurer in 2025, with a 5.6% share of GWP.

The insurer’s capitalization has been strong compared with rated non-life peers. Its RBC ratio has been above 240% over 2023-2025 and at 241% at end-1H26. Its operating performance has improved, with annualized ROE rising to 12% in 1H26 from 6% in 2025 and exceeding the three-year average of 8%, driven by stronger earnings from tighter underwriting and better investment returns. People’s Insurance’s combined ratio improved to 102% in 1H26, while its three-year average of 113% remained elevated, although below the industry average.

CICPLC

The upgrade reflects CICPLC’s ‘Moderate’ company profile, recovering profitability and satisfactory capitalization.

Fitch has revised CICPLC’s corporate governance assessment to ‘Neutral’ from ‘Less Favorable’, reflecting measures taken over the past two years to address prior weaknesses in its governance structure. CICPLC has an adequate franchise, supported by co-operative-society ownership, with a 3% share of non-life GWP and its position as the tenth-largest insurer in Sri Lanka in 2025.

CICPLC’s operating performance has strengthened from weak historical levels, with annualized ROE rising to 6% in 1H26 from a three-year average of 0.3% and the combined ratio improving to 109% in 1H26, from 115% in 2025. However, profitability and underwriting performance remain weaker than those of higher-rated Fitch-rated domestic non-life peers. Capitalization is satisfactory, with the RBC ratio remaining above 200% in 2023-2025 and standing at 210% at end-1H26.

CILL

CILL’s rating reflects its moderate company profile and satisfactory regulatory capital position, which are offset by its weaker underwriting performance relative to peers.

CILL was the seventh-largest non-life insurer in Sri Lanka in 2025, with a GWP market share of 6.8%. Its business mix is more diversified than that of most domestic non-life insurers, reflecting its larger presence in non-motor business lines. Its regulatory capitalization remained satisfactory, with an RBC ratio of 222% at end-1H26 (end-2025: 230%).

CILL’s underwriting performance weakened in 2025. The combined ratio rose to 119% from 100% in 2024, due to high medical claims and adverse claims development in health. This resulted in a net loss of LKR654 million in 2025 (2024: profit of LKR436 million). Its recent performance has been weak relative to Fitch-rated domestic non-life insurers, with the combined ratio at 113% in 1H26. CILL’s continued losses could weaken its regulatory capitalization.

Ownership of CILL is in the process of being transferred from Melstacorp PLC (National Long-Term Rating: AAA(lka)/Stable) to Janashakthi PLC. Janashakthi proposes to initially acquire an 81% stake in CILL, with the remaining 19% to be transferred in two tranches of 9% and 10% over the subsequent two years. The transaction remains subject to final approval from the Insurance Regulatory Commission of Sri Lanka.

CGF

The affirmation reflects CGF’s ‘Moderate’ company profile and improving operating conditions in Sri Lanka’s construction sector, which are offset by CGF’s historically volatile performance.

CGF is fully state-owned, with the Secretary to the Treasury acting as the trust’s settlor. It serves a niche market by providing guarantees and related services to SME contractors involved in government projects.

A growing foreign-funded infrastructure pipeline supported demand for CGF’s bonds and guarantees, driving a material recovery in core guarantee income in 1H26. CGF’s average ROE was 13% in 2023-2025, although investment income, rather than guarantee operations, remained the main contributor to profitability.

Capitalization was adequate, supported by internally generated surplus and total capital of about LKR2.0 billion at end-2025. Net guarantee risk exposure was modest at 0.6x total equity. However, CGF’s earnings and business volumes remain sensitive to the pace of project implementation and broader conditions in the domestic construction sector.

RATING SENSITIVITIES
Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Negative Rating Action/Downgrade
SLIC Life

– Prolonged weakness in financial performance;

– A deterioration in the RBC ratio to below 300% for a sustained period;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign, which account for a large share of SLIC Life’s investment portfolio.

SLIC General

– Sustained weakness in financial performance;

– Deterioration in the RBC ratio to below 220% for a sustained period;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign, which account for a large share of SLIC General’s investment portfolio.

HNB Life and HNBGI

– Deterioration in HNB Life’s RBC ratio to below 240% or a significant deterioration in HNBGI’s capital position for a sustained period;

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance or weaker risk-management practices;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign.

CICPLC

– Deterioration in the company profile, including a weaker franchise and competitive positioning, or Fitch’s perception that the insurer’s corporate governance practices have deteriorated;

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance, or weaker risk-management practices;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign.

CILL

– Deterioration in the company profile, including a weaker franchise and competitive positioning, or Fitch’s perception that the insurer’s corporate governance practices have deteriorated;

– Deterioration in the RBC ratio to below 220% for a sustained period;

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance, or weaker risk-management practices;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including downgrades of the ratings on the Sri Lanka sovereign or domestic financial institutions.

People’s Insurance

– Deterioration in the regulatory RBC ratio to below 200% for a sustained period;

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance or weaker risk-management practices;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings on Sri Lankan financial institutions or the sovereign.

CGF

– Sustained deterioration in financial performance or weaker risk-management practices;

– Deterioration in the company profile, for instance, due to a significant weakening in CGF’s association with the government, or deterioration in its business risk profile due to a decline in the country’s economic conditions that affects the domestic construction sector;

– Rising investment and asset risks, including a downgrade of the ratings of financial institutions or the sovereign.

Factors that Could, Individually or Collectively, Lead to Positive Rating Action/Upgrade
SLIC Life

– Further improvement in the company profile, including a greater operating scale and a stronger market positioning

SLIC General

– Further improvement in the company profile, including a greater operating scale and stronger market position;

– An improvement in the risk-based capital ratio to well above 300% while maintaining the combined ratio at below 95%.

HNB Life and HNBGI

– An improvement in the RBC ratio to well above 320% at HNB Life and 250% at HNBGI, while maintaining the combined ratio below 98% for HNBGI;

– Further improvement in the company profile, for instance, from a stronger business franchise and larger operating scale.

CICPLC

– Further improvement in the company profile, including a stronger business franchise and greater operating scale;

– Maintaining its combined ratio well below 105% for a sustained period, while our assessment of the insurer’s capitalization remains unchanged.

CILL

– Maintaining its combined ratio below 98% for a sustained period, while our assessment of the insurer’s capitalization remains unchanged.

– Sustained improvement in the company profile, including a further expansion in its operating scale and business franchise

People’s Insurance

– An improvement in the RBC ratio to well above 240% and maintaining the combined ratio below 98% consistently for a sustained period;

– Improving the business profile in terms of broader diversification of business lines.

CGF

– Sustained improvement in the company profile in terms of a larger operating scale and successful diversification into profitable and stable business lines.

item.title: Sri Lanka stocks close up 0.66-pct led by banks
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Positive contributors to the ASPI were Commercial Bank, Hatton National Bank, Sri Lanka Telecom, Distilleries Company
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Colombo Stock Exchange closed up on Thursday, CSE data showed, with the benchmark All Share Price Index moving up 0.66 percent.

The ASPI was up 140.36 points at 21,543.12, while the more liquid S&P SL20 was up 0.85 percent, or 52.07 points, at 6,149.04.

Positive contributors to the ASPI were Commercial Bank of Ceylon (up 0.94 percent at 215.25 rupees), Hatton National Bank (up 0.95 percent at 397 rupees), Sri Lanka Telecom (up 4.94 percent at 93.50 rupees), Distilleries Company of Sri Lanka (up 0.86 percent at 58.60 rupees), and LOLC Holdings (up 2.01 percent at 405.75 rupees).

Hayleys (down 0.75 percent at 232.25 rupees), Bukit Darah (down 2.27 percent at 840 rupees), Richard Pieris and Company (down 1.82 percent at 27 rupees), Malwatte Valley Plantation (down 3.30 percent at 52.80 rupees), and Ambeon Holdings (down 1.44 percent at 34.30 rupees) were top negative contributors.

Market turnover was 1.73 billion rupees. Banks led turnover with 888.06 million rupees. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka marine industry seeks alternative coastal sites amid Colombo Port space crunch
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: They also flagged taxation structures and Harmonized System (HS) code classifications
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s marine-based industries are seeking alternative coastal sites for shipbuilding and repairs as severe space constraints inside the Colombo Port limit expansion, the Export Development Board (EDB) said after meeting industry representatives.

Stakeholders raised the shortage of suitable industrial space for fabrication, vessel assembly, storage, and sea trials during the inaugural meeting of the EDB’s Advisory Committee on Marine-Based Industries.

They also flagged taxation structures and Harmonized System (HS) code classifications applied to locally manufactured commercial boats sold to domestic tourism operators as key policy issues requiring review.

To address infrastructure gaps and expand marine tourism, the committee discussed developing sheltered anchorages, boatyards, and marinas in coastal hubs such as Galle, alongside reviewing progress on the proposed Kapparathota Marina Development Project.

Chaired by Kaushal Rajapaksha with Ricky Barnett as Co-Chairman, the committee plans to set up seven specialized subcommittees — covering shipbuilding, boat manufacturing, regulatory affairs, skills training, offshore services, nautical tourism, and export promotion — to align with the National Export Development Plan (2026–2030) and pitch investment-ready projects at Sri Lanka Expo 2027. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka public sector unions mobilize over 2026 budget pay anomalies as inflation bites
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: "Increasing salaries in accordance with the cost of living has not been done yet
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s National People’s Power government is facing widening trade union protests across the public sector after its 2026 budget failed to resolve long-standing salary anomalies or compensate state workers for rising living costs, even as ministers urged unions to await a commission report next year.

Living costs have climbed sharply, with inflation reaching 8.3 percent in October after the rupee depreciated.

The Janatha Vimukthi Peramuna (JVP), the main party in the NPP, was heavily involved in trade union action for nearly three decades.

Until winning the presidency in 2024, organizing strikes, protests, and work stoppages was one of the party’s primary methods for exerting political influence.

Education unions mobilize

Dissatisfaction has boiled over in the education sector, where seven major principals’ unions and nearly 20 teachers’ unions have organized a “black protest” for November 23.

Union leaders accused the administration of failing to allocate funds to eliminate teacher-principal salary disparities or establish a promised professionals’ council.

“As trade unions, we are putting forward the demand that an interim allowance of 25,000 rupees must be granted to all of them,” Graded Principals’ Union General Secretary Nimal Mudunkotuwa said.

Sri Lanka Government Teachers’ Union General Secretary Nalaka de Silva warned that educators, from preschools to universities, would escalate industrial action if the government continued delaying a settlement.

“They came to power promising that they would resolve the teachers’ salary anomaly in the very first budget. We will definitely go on a one-day token strike,” de Silva told reporters.

Government admits cost-of-living gap

Unrest has also spread to irrigation engineers — who fall under the Ministry of Agriculture, Livestock, Land and Irrigation — and veterinarians, both of whom are taking trade union action over severe staff shortages, difficulties running state institutions, and professionals leaving the country.

Speaking during the 2026 budget debate in parliament on Thursday, Minister K D Lalkantha said veterinarians’ demand to add an extra working hour was fair, but warned that granting isolated concessions through the budget would destabilize the entire state sector.

“However, if we lay hands on any one place in the public service to find a separate answer, the entire public service will go into a serious mess,” Lalkantha said.

Lalkantha, who noted he has worked with trade unions since 1996 and acknowledged that public servants made a major sacrifice via postal votes to elect the administration, explained that unions have long campaigned on two national demands: adding all allowances to the basic salary and raising pay in line with living costs.

While saying the government fulfilled the first demand across three budgets, he admitted it has yet to meet the second.

“Even though we increased basic salaries in the public service, increasing salaries in accordance with the cost of living has not been done yet. We accept that,” Lalkantha told parliament.

Pointing to the country’s 2022 economic collapse, Lalkantha said Sri Lanka needs a strong, efficient, target-driven public service rather than simply a massive workforce, adding that executing allocated budget funds on time remains a major challenge.

He urged unions to bring their service-minute disputes and pay anomalies to a 15-member Salaries Commission appointed on July 2 under retired Special Grade administrative officer Asoka Peiris.

The commission has already received submissions from 69 unions ahead of a December 31 deadline and must submit its report by June next year.

Lalkantha also acknowledged that doubling existing office allowances by 100 percent in the budget had preserved grassroots disparities among four categories of officers working in the same Grama Niladhari divisions.

While rural and urban office allowances rose from 2,000 to 4,000 rupees and 3,000 to 6,000 rupees for Grama Niladharis and agricultural research and production assistants (Kupanisas), and from 2,000 to 4,000 rupees and 2,500 to 5,000 rupees for Samurdhi officers, graduate Development Officers saw theirs rise from just 750 to 1,500 rupees and 1,000 to 2,000 rupees. Lalkantha noted this created a dignity issue for Development Officers and admitted that giving equal increases to unequal bases only recreated inequality.

 Opposition alleges ‘numbers game’

Samagi Jana Balawegaya lawmaker Ranjith Madduma Bandara countered that 85 percent of public servants had backed the government through postal votes expecting relief, but were instead handed a “numbers game”.

He said the government merely absorbed existing allowances totaling 15,300 rupees into basic pay, resulting in cumulative three-year increases of just 60 percent for office aides, 68 percent for management assistants, and 71 percent for development officers, while leaving engineers’ 15,000-to-20,000-rupee field allowances unrestored.

“Having added this, today there is no cost-of-living allowance. You played a numbers game. You deceived the public servants,” Madduma Bandara said during the parliamentary debate.

With police facing a 30,000-officer shortage and unions across health, engineering, and education mobilizing, the government faces growing pressure to deliver interim relief before the Salaries Commission finalizes its recommendations next year. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka central bank seeks firm to manage staff competency assessments
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: From professional firms to design, develop, implement, and manage competency assessments through assessment centres.
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – The Central Bank of Sri Lanka (CBSL) has invited proposals from professional firms to design, develop, implement, and manage competency assessments through assessment centres.

Bidding documents are available on bank working days from November 19 to December 9, between 10 am and 3 pm, upon a written request on a business letterhead sent to procsec@cbsl.lk.

A pre-bid meeting is scheduled for December 1, at 10 am on the ground floor of the CBSL Head Office Building at No. 30, Janadhipathi Mawatha, Colombo 1.

Bids close on December 10, at 2:30 pm, with bid opening taking place afterward at the CBSL Head Office.

Further details are available on the Central Bank of Sri Lanka tenders portal. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s COPA approves Rs65.09mn write-off of legacy agriculture losses
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Across four longstanding advance accounts belonging to the Department of Agriculture
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s parliamentary Committee on Public Accounts (COPA) has approved the write-off of 65.09 million rupees in unauthorized working losses across four longstanding advance accounts belonging to the Department of Agriculture, a parliament statement said.

The decision was taken at a meeting held on November 17, chaired by Member of Parliament Kabir Hashim.

The committee reviewed and agreed to settle long-standing losses and balance discrepancies in the following accounts:
– Agricultural Repair Workshop: 35.7 million rupees
– Potato Cultivation Extension Programme: 23.97 million rupees (a programme concluded in 1996)
– Welisara Agricultural Workshop: 5 million rupees
– Narahenpita Agricultural Central Stores: 421,884 rupees

Following a review of the facts presented, COPA approved the write-off of the recorded losses and instructed officials to rectify the balance discrepancies.

The committee also stressed the need to maintain proper accounting records, follow audit procedures, and strengthen financial controls to prevent similar issues from recurring. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka budget preserves debt reduction path: Fitch Ratings
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: Forecast government debt will drop to about 92% of GDP in 2026, from 115% in 2022, but well above the 55% median for ‘B’
item.content:encoded:
Sri Lanka’s 2027 budget signals the government’s ongoing commitment to fiscal discipline and debt reduction while accommodating higher spending on investment and cyclone reconstruction, Fitch Ratings says. Fiscal discipline, demonstrated again by the outperformance of fiscal targets in 2026, and a focus on debt reduction were key factors behind our upgrade of the sovereign rating to ‘B-‌’/Stable from ‘CCC+’ in September.

The budget targets a primary surplus of 2.3% of GDP, down from an estimated 3.6% in 2026. The 2026 surplus is well above the 2.5% target in last year’s budget and our earlier 2.6% forecast, reflecting stronger revenue. The decline in the surplus in 2027 reflects lower revenue and higher capital spending but remains consistent with a debt reduction path. This implies a 2027 deficit of 4.5% of GDP, wider than the 3.7% in 2026.

Budget assumptions appear credible and broadly align with our forecasts from our September sovereign review. The 2027 primary-surplus target is slightly below our 2.8% forecast because planned spending is higher than we assumed. However, we think there is potential for further under-execution on capex again this year, which could drive a slightly higher surplus.

Primary expenditure is budgeted at 13.6% of GDP in 2027, above the 13% statutory ceiling under the 2024 Public Finance Management Act (PFMA). The temporary deviation from the PFMA mainly reflects capital spending for reconstruction following Cyclone Ditwah, as well as higher public capex plans.

The plans include LKR260 billion carried forward from a supplementary budget for cyclone reconstruction passed in December 2025 but not spent in 2026 as a result of under-execution. This is the second year the government has sought a deviation from the PFMA, although budget under-execution meant the ceiling was not actually breached in 2026.

Sustaining recent revenue gains will help underpin strong primary surpluses. Revenue is budgeted to moderate to 15.8% of GDP in 2027 from 16.6% in 2026 and 16.7% in 2025, as the boost to import-duty collections from pent-up vehicle-import demand fades as imports normalise. However, efforts to broaden the tax base and improve compliance are supporting more broad-based revenue improvements.

The budget is broadly aligned with International Monetary Fund programme parameters. This should support the seventh review of Sri Lanka’s Extended Fund Facility. The current programme ends in March 2027, and the government announced the establishment of a committee to assess a potential follow-on arrangement, which could provide a further policy anchor.

Sustained efforts to cement revenue gains and expenditure restraint will remain central to achieving ongoing debt reduction and for the future path of the sovereign rating.

Over the medium term, the government aims to maintain a primary surplus of 3.0% of GDP, requiring politically difficult trade-offs to comply with the 13% expenditure ceiling under the PFMA.

Efforts to boost investment spending could help lift potential GDP growth, which we forecast at 4.2%, and support steady fiscal outcomes. However, this will depend on capex execution, effective targeting and progress on broader structural reforms.

Fiscal vulnerabilities remain high despite the substantial fiscal adjustment achieved in the past few years. We forecast government debt will drop to about 92% of GDP in 2026, from 115% in 2022, but well above the 55% median for ‘B’ rated sovereigns.

We expect interest payments to decline to around 41.0% of revenue in 2026 from nearly 80% in 2023, but remain more than three times the 12.7% ‘B’ median. A lengthening record of fiscal policy credibility and healthy primary surpluses will likely be critical towards ensuring debt sustainability and supporting potential future rating momentum.

item.title: Sri Lanka’s UDA fails to attract promised $500mn foreign investment, shifts screening to BOI
item.dc:creator: Ranul Seneviratne
item.description: Prompting plans to hand investor financial screening over to the Board of Investment (BOI).
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Sri Lanka’s Urban Development Authority (UDA) has failed to bring in any of the 500 million US dollars in foreign investment it pledged for 2026, prompting plans to hand investor financial screening over to the Board of Investment (BOI).

Appearing before a parliamentary sectoral oversight committee, UDA officials admitted that zero dollars had materialized so far out of the 500-million-dollar target, blaming regional conflict in West Asia for forcing the cancellation of a planned investment forum.

Committee lawmakers criticized the agency’s approach, noting that Port City had successfully held its own investment forum in Dubai, and argued that hosting investor forums locally attracts middlemen rather than genuine foreign capital.

“Instead of attracting real investors, it looked like you were going to attract brokers, because investors do not come from inside Sri Lanka,” the committee chairman S M Marikkar said.

The Urban Development sector recorded only 26 percent spending progress during the first 10 months of the year, with the UDA itself reaching 19 percent and forecasting just 35 percent by the end of December.

Officials attributed the slow progress to delays in planning new projects introduced through the Budget Speech, such as the Life Cities program, as well as slow execution on foreign-funded housing schemes where two contracts had to be terminated.

To remove bottlenecks in land allocation, the UDA Chairman M G Hemachandra said a Cabinet paper is moving forward so that the BOI will assess investors’ financial capacity while the UDA focuses strictly on releasing land.

“Previously, two places were checking the investor’s financial capability—both us and the BOI—so we submitted a Cabinet paper to hand that task to the BOI,” Hemachandra said.

The UDA will also launch a public website next week listing all available state lands, zoning rules, and master plan details for mixed or transit-oriented development so foreign investors can review opportunities before visiting Sri Lanka.

Meanwhile, the committee directed the ministry to wind up inactive state companies such as Sahaspura Investment Limited and Selendiva Investments Limited, warning that keeping unutilized entities or idle staff on public books is unacceptable. (Colombo/Nov19/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka Customs achieves over 59-pct of November 2026 target in 16 days
item.dc:creator: Shihar Aneez
item.description: The Customs revenue likely to hit fresh record of over 2,700 bln in 2026, analysts expect
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Revenue collected by Sri Lanka Customs in the first 15 days of November accounted for over 59 percent of the month’s target, official data showed, with the island nation poised to see a fresh record high revenue this year.

The revenue collecting body has surpassed monthly targets for 10 straight months through October.

Customs’ October revenue target was set at 194.5 billion rupees. But the revenue collecting body already collected 115.5 billion rupees in the first 16 days of this month, official data showed.

It has already achieved 111.3 percent of this year’s target through November 16, official data showed.

Customs has been accelerating container clearance using digital scanning to reduce corruption and fast-track the clearance process.

Last year, Customs collected a record 2,551 billion rupees in revenues, higher than a revised target of 2,241 billion rupees for the year, achieving 64.2 percent higher revenue than the previous year’s revenue of 1,553 million rupees.

Customs has set a revenue target of 2,207 billion rupees for this year, 13.5 percent less than last year as it expects a significant decline in car imports. However, it has already achieved 2,456.8 1 billion rupees through November 16.

Sri Lanka Customs’ revenue jump is largely due to stronger enforcement, improved valuation practices, and a rebound in import volumes after years of contraction.

Following the economic crisis of 2022, imports fell sharply as the country imposed restrictions to conserve foreign exchange.

However, with the stabilization of reserves, the relaxation of certain import controls, and a steady recovery in consumer demand, customs collections from import duties, excise, and other levies have risen.

Officials note that tighter monitoring of under-invoicing and misdeclaration of goods has also contributed to boosting state revenue.

The combined effect of increased import activity, currency movements, and stricter enforcement has positioned Customs as one of the top revenue sources for the Treasury in 2025, providing a vital cushion as the state works to meet fiscal targets under the IMF-supported program. (Colombo/November 18/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka’s Union Bank to seek shareholder approval for Rs708mn rights issue
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: On the basis of one new share for every 16 existing shares held
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Union Bank of Colombo PLC has called an extraordinary general meeting on December 3 to seek shareholder approval for a proposed rights issue aimed at raising up to 708.4 million rupees.

The bank plans to issue up to 67.7 million new ordinary voting shares at 10.46 rupees each on the basis of one new share for every 16 existing shares held as of December 7, 2026, which has been set as the record date.

The proposed rights issue will be considered at a virtual extraordinary general meeting to be streamed from the bank’s head office in Colombo.

According to the market filing, shareholders who apply for additional shares may receive allocations from rights not taken up by existing shareholders, including shares arising from fractional entitlements.

Any remaining unsubscribed shares may be allotted at the board’s discretion to persons disclosed in the shareholder circular, at the same rights issue price. (Colombo/Nov18/2026)

item.title: Sri Lanka regulator fines two institutions Rs3.3mn for AML/CFT lapses
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The penalties were imposed under the Financial Transactions Reporting Act
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – The Sri Lanka Central Bank’s Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU) has imposed administrative penalties totaling 3.3 million rupees on two reporting institutions between April and June 2026 for breaches of anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) regulations.

The penalties were imposed under the Financial Transactions Reporting Act (FTRA), with the FIU saying the sanctions were aimed at enforcing compliance with AML/CFT requirements, CBSL said.

Commercial Credit and Finance PLC was fined 3 million rupees after the FIU found that the company had established and maintained business relationships with a person designated under United Nations sanctions-related regulations.

According to the FIU, the company had failed to effectively verify a customer at the time of establishing the business relationship, failed to adequately screen its existing customer database against updated designated-persons lists, and did not update relevant sanctions lists in its systems without delay.

The shortcomings were identified during an onsite spot examination by the FIU.

The penalty was imposed on April 9, and paid on April 21, the central bank said.

Meanwhile, New Natasha (Pvt) Ltd was fined 300,000 rupees for multiple compliance deficiencies identified during a risk-based onsite examination conducted by the Central Bank’s Department of Foreign Exchange and subsequently communicated to the FIU.

The FIU said the company had failed to obtain mandatory customer information, including the purpose of transactions, source of funds and politically exposed person status during customer due diligence procedures for transactions above 200,000 rupees.

It had also failed to retain copies of customer identification documents, conduct a comprehensive money laundering and terrorist financing risk assessment, and screen customers against designated sanctions lists.

The regulator noted, however, that the examination did not reveal any business relationships with designated individuals or entities despite the procedural and system weaknesses.

The penalty on New Natasha was imposed on May 15, and paid on June 3.

The money collected was credited to the Consolidated Fund.

The FIU, Sri Lanka’s AML/CFT regulator, said penalties are determined after considering the nature and gravity of non-compliance by reporting institutions. (Colombo/Nov18/2026)

item.title: Women in Tech Sri Lanka signs MoU with IIT to boost tech talent
item.dc:creator: Nirmalie Alahakone
item.description: The agreement establishes a framework for long-term collaboration between academia and industry
item.content:encoded:
ECONOMYNEXT – Women in Tech Sri Lanka has signed an agreement with the Informatics Institute of Technology (IIT Campus), in collaboration with LeapGen, to strengthen technology education, research, innovation and women’s participation in the technology sector, the organizations said.

The agreement establishes a framework for long-term collaboration between academia and industry, with a focus on developing industry-ready talent, expanding educational opportunities and supporting innovation within Sri Lanka’s technology ecosystem.

Under the partnership, the organizations plan to undertake collaborative research and publications, facilitate student internships and industry projects, and promote knowledge-sharing through professional events, expert lectures and faculty development programmes.

The initiative will also support curriculum enhancement, entrepreneurship and community outreach activities aimed at strengthening links between academia and industry, while providing students and young professionals with greater access to practical experience and professional networks.

The partners said a key objective of the collaboration is to help build a more inclusive and future-ready technology workforce by aligning academic learning with industry requirements.

Through joint programmes, Women in Tech Sri Lanka, IIT and LeapGen aim to encourage innovation, nurture emerging talent and create more opportunities for women and girls pursuing careers in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM).

The partnership also supports Women in Tech’s global mission of empowering five million women and girls in STEM by 2030 through increased access to education, mentorship, skills development and career advancement opportunities. (Colombo/Nov18/2026)
